target: AG1’s claim that AI’s convenience, health, work, accessibility, and safety benefits show it is good for society.
objection: AI is not good for society overall because its benefits come with systemic risks that can outweigh them, including privacy harms, unsafe health guidance, weakened critical thinking, accessibility limits, and racial bias.

target: AG2’s assumption that AI’s core operation necessarily depends on intensive personal-data profiling and therefore inherently creates dominant privacy harm.
objection: AI can provide useful everyday and safety-related functions without pervasive profiling by using on-device/local inference, federated learning, differential privacy, anonymization, consent, and data minimization, so privacy harm is not an unavoidable feature of AI itself.

target: AG1’s claim that AI makes everyday life, health, work, accessibility, and safety better overall.
objection: Those benefits are typically inseparable from major tradeoffs—especially privacy surveillance, unsafe health advice, erosion of critical thinking, unequal accessibility, and biased treatment of racial minorities—so AI is not net good for society.

target: AG2’s broad claim that AI’s social benefits are typically inseparable from major privacy harms.
objection: AI can achieve convenience and safety with far less personal data through local processing, privacy-preserving learning, and data-minimization policies, so the privacy-harm tradeoff is not inherent or inevitable.

target: AG1’s overall positive framing of AI’s convenience, health, work, accessibility, and safety benefits.
objection: AI’s real-world operation often produces recurring tradeoffs: it depends on extensive data capture, can give wrong health guidance, can weaken critical thinking, can be unreliable for accessibility, and can amplify racial bias, making the net social effect negative.

target: AG2’s assumption that AI’s harms are effectively unavoidable and therefore outweigh its benefits.
objection: Privacy, health, job-displacement, critical-thinking, and bias harms can be reduced through governance and design—such as minimization, human oversight, retraining, tutor-style prompting, and fairness audits—so those harms do not necessarily dominate AI’s benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that AI makes work and learning easier in a way that is socially good overall.
objection: AI often undermines critical thinking and judgment by encouraging epistemic dependence on opaque outputs, reducing people’s practice in verifying claims and reasoning independently, which creates long-run learning and reasoning harm.

target: AG2’s claim that AI typically causes epistemic dependence and weakens critical thinking.
objection: AI can be used to strengthen critical thinking by acting as a tutor, providing source-grounded and uncertainty-aware answers, and integrating with fact-checking workflows that train users to verify claims instead of accepting outputs blindly.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s work-related benefits make it socially good overall.
objection: In practice, AI often automates and displaces white-collar and service work, weakens worker bargaining power, and concentrates gains in large firms with the resources to adopt it, so it can harm the economic well-being of many people and businesses.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is mainly labor-replacing and concentrated among large firms.
objection: AI often augments workers rather than replacing them, creates complementary roles, and is increasingly accessible through off-the-shelf services, so productivity gains need not be concentrated only in large companies or produce net job loss as the dominant effect.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s everyday convenience and productivity gains make it socially beneficial.
objection: AI makes impersonation, fake messages, and fraudulent media cheap and scalable, increasing deception, privacy violations, business losses, and the burden of constant verification, so its harms can outweigh its benefits.

target: AG2’s claim that AI-enabled deception and fraud are an unmitigated dominant harm.
objection: AI is also widely used to detect phishing, suspicious activity, account takeovers, and deepfakes, so it can substantially improve fraud prevention and authenticity verification rather than merely enabling scams.

target: AG1’s workplace-safety-and-convenience framing.
objection: AI is often deployed as algorithmic workplace control that monitors employee behavior and productivity in opaque ways, reduces autonomy, increases stress and insecurity, and therefore harms workers rather than making work broadly easier.

target: AG2’s assumption that workplace AI monitoring is inherently harmful and inseparable from AI safety/efficiency benefits.
objection: AI workplace systems can improve safety without employee surveillance, and when monitoring exists it can be constrained by privacy-by-design, transparency, limits on automated discipline, and worker contestability, so harmful algorithmic management is not inevitable.

target: AG1’s claim that AI benefits society in high-stakes domains such as services, employment, education, and health.
objection: AI often makes important decisions through opaque reasoning that people cannot meaningfully interpret or challenge, so errors and abuses persist and accountability weakens, undermining social well-being.

target: AG2’s claim that opacity in high-stakes AI means errors and abuses cannot be corrected.
objection: Contestability can be engineered through human review, decision records, explanations, audits, and appeal processes, so high-stakes AI need not leave mistakes and abuses uncorrected.

target: AG1’s claim that high-stakes AI can be meaningfully contested and corrected.
objection: In practice, explanations are often post-hoc or incomplete, organizations withhold needed evidence and model details for privacy or trade-secret reasons, and appeals are too limited or slow, so effective contestability is often only nominal.

target: AG2’s claim that high-stakes AI typically leaves mistakes and abuses uncorrected because contestability is unavailable.
objection: Institutions can require decision records, actionable explanations, and independent audits under confidentiality, so meaningful challenge and correction are feasible even when full model internals are not public.

target: AG1’s claim that contestability does not require full disclosure of model internals.
objection: Meaningful contesting requires verifiable evidence about the model’s true decision basis; post-hoc explanations, restricted access to data and internals, and confidentiality-limited audits usually prevent challengers from proving or correcting the actual cause of a bad decision.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy and proprietary limits make contestability effectively impossible in high-stakes AI.
objection: High-stakes AI can be governed through due-process-style procedures, documented decision bases, external oversight, and accountability by regulators or courts, so opacity does not automatically make appeals nominal.

target: AG1’s claim that procedural safeguards can reliably produce meaningful contestability.
objection: Decision summaries, post-hoc explanations, and oversight under confidentiality often do not provide the verifiable evidence needed for a real appeal, and appeals are too slow or narrow to correct harm promptly, so contestability is often only formal.

target: AG2’s claim that high-stakes AI usually leaves mistakes and abuses effectively uncorrected.
objection: Meaningful contestability can be built through actionably documented decision bases, human-in-the-loop review, clear appeals, and regulated oversight, so high-stakes AI need not leave harmful outcomes uncorrected.

target: AG1’s claim that people can get enough evidence for meaningful contest and correction in high-stakes AI even without access to internals.
objection: Limited records and explanations are often insufficient for verifying the true causal basis of a decision, and auditors still lack the data and provenance needed to resolve individual disputes, so contestability remains weak in practice.

target: AG2’s claim that high-stakes AI inevitably leaves preventable harms uncorrected.
objection: Continuous monitoring, incident response, and post-deployment revision can detect drift and abuse and then roll back or patch systems, so harms need not persist simply because individual contestability is limited.

target: AG1’s claim that monitoring and incident response can correct major harms without relying on contestability.
objection: Many high-stakes harms are hard to observe in aggregate, may only become visible through affected individuals’ reports, and require case-specific evidence that operators lack, so contestability is often necessary for detection and correction.

target: AG2’s claim that limited individual contestability means preventable harms persist.
objection: Pre-deployment validation, bias/error testing, and real-time safety metrics can prevent and correct many failures before they become persistent harms, so limited user contestability does not imply uncorrected abuses.

target: AG1’s claim that safety metrics and rollback mechanisms are usually enough to correct harmful outcomes.
objection: Benchmarks miss long-tail and out-of-distribution failures, metrics often fail to capture discrimination or procedural unfairness, and rollback or patching can be too slow or costly, so many harms persist without meaningful contestability.

target: AG2’s claim that opacity means high-stakes AI leaves harms uncorrected.
objection: High-stakes AI often remains contestable because a human decision-maker can be held accountable, provide evidence-based justification, and review appeals, so opacity of model internals does not automatically make appeals nominal.

target: AG1’s human-in-the-loop accountability argument.
objection: The accountable human often merely repeats the AI’s recommendation and cannot independently reconstruct the model’s basis, so an appeal to human responsibility still leaves decisions effectively uncheckable and contestability nominal.
